# Start here

Internal. Last checked against the live MPP controller (v0.6.3) and Crucible v0.6.4 on 2026-11-11.

This guide takes you from no access at all to writing, launching and debugging your own Crucible workflows, with the runs landing on the pirate cluster. It assumes nothing. If a step looks obvious, do it anyway. Most first-day failures come from a skipped "obvious" step.

Each tab is one step. Do the first five in order; the rest are there when you need them.

* Start here: what Crucible is and where it lives.  
* Access: what to ask for before anything else, and the three ways to drive Crucible.  
* Setup: API key, desktop app, CLIs, your agent, your editor. About 30 minutes.  
* First launches: two tiny packs that prove your setup works end to end.  
* Authoring loop: the edit, push, preview, launch cycle you will repeat.  
* Writing workflows: the DSL you will use in the first month.  
* Running on pirate: GPUs, builds, Kueue, providers and watching pods.  
* Running on pirate 2: the second cluster, what it has and what it lacks.  
* Agent drafting (provisional): an unreleased desktop app feature where a local agent edits your draft for you.  
* Builds and GPU Jobs: how a pack builds an image with buildit and runs it on a GPU through Kueue.  
* Hill climb example: a real GPU workflow, start to finish.  
* Debugging runs: where to look when a run fails.  
* Going further and Reference: everything else.

## What Crucible is

Crucible is a deterministic agent orchestrator with native sandboxing. You describe a workflow as a small graph of tasks. Some tasks are plain scripts (`command`). Others are agent turns (`agent` or `skill`), which run a coding agent such as Claude Code inside a locked-down sandbox. Crucible runs the graph, moves outputs between tasks, enforces a cost and time ceiling, and records everything the run did.

A cluster is a pool of machines, and a pod is one program running on it. Both words, and the other Kubernetes terms this guide uses, are explained under Kubernetes in five minutes, below.

You never run the engine on the cluster yourself. A controller (the MPP deployment) owns launches. You hand it a pack and a few choices. It starts a pod on a cluster (pirate), and that pod runs the graph and reports back.

### Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| Pack | A directory with `crucible.toml` (settings, in [TOML](https://toml.io/)), `workflow.star` (the task graph, in [Starlark](https://github.com/bazelbuild/starlark/blob/master/spec.md), a small Python dialect) and whatever files the tasks need. This is what you write. |
| Playbook | A pack registered on the controller from a Git repo, launchable by its team. |
| Draft | A pack you are still editing, stored on the controller under your name. It launches like a playbook. Every save is a new numbered version. |
| Launch | One request to run a playbook or draft, with param values and ceilings. It shows up as a key like `playbook:<id>:<suffix>`. |
| Run | The execution a launch produced, with a run id and a short name (for example `maximal-koi`). |
| Task | One node in the graph. `command` runs a script; `agent` and `skill` run an agent turn. |
| Sandbox | The isolated pod an agent turn runs in. It cannot reach the network except for an allowlist. |
| Loop pod | The pod that runs the engine and every `command` task for one run (`crucible-run-<name>` on pirate). |
| Provider | A registered model endpoint plus the harness that drives it (for example `enmaas`, harness `claude`). |
| Harness | The agent CLI inside the sandbox: `claude`, `codex`, `opencode` or `pi`. |
| Dispatch target | The cluster a launch runs on. Today on MPP: `pirate` (the default), `pirate2`, `hub` or a personal kubeconfig target. |
| Ceilings | The `max cost` (USD) and `max time` you set per launch. The run stops when it hits either. |

### The three-part mental model

1\. You write a pack on your laptop, in any editor.

2\. The controller stores it as a draft (or registers it as a playbook) and launches it with your choices: params, ceilings, dispatch target, provider and model.

3\. Pirate runs it. The loop pod runs your commands, and each agent turn gets its own sandbox pod. GPU work waits its turn in [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/overview/), the cluster's GPU queue. Container image builds go through buildit, a build service that runs [Buildah](https://buildah.io/) on the cluster. Results come back to the controller, where you read them in the desktop app, the web UI or the CLI.

 `your laptop                    MPP controller (hub)                   pirate (spoke)`  
 `-----------                    --------------------                   --------------`  
 `pack dir  --draft push------>  draft vN  --launch------------------>  crucible-system/crucible-run-<name>   (engine + command tasks)`  
 `desktop app / web / crux       params, ceilings, provider, target      crucible-sandboxes/...                 (agent sandbox pods)`  
          `<----run log, graph, files, cost-----------------------------  crucible-builds/buildit-*              (container builds)`  
                                                                          `crucible-kueue-e2e/<jobs>              (GPU Jobs via Kueue)`

### Kubernetes in five minutes

You do not need to operate Kubernetes to use Crucible. You do need about a dozen words, because they show up in logs, in error messages and in the rest of this guide. Skip this if you already know them.

| Term | Plain meaning | Upstream docs |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Kubernetes | Software that runs programs across a pool of machines. You say what you want to run, and it picks a machine, starts the program and restarts or reports it when it stops. | [Overview](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/) |
| Cluster | One pool of machines managed by one Kubernetes installation. Pirate is a cluster. Pirate 2 and MPP are different clusters. | [Cluster architecture](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/) |
| OpenShift | Red Hat's distribution of Kubernetes. Both clusters run it. Its command-line client is `oc`, which accepts everything `kubectl` (the stock Kubernetes client) does. | [oc CLI](https://docs.okd.io/latest/cli_reference/openshift_cli/getting-started-cli.html) |
| Node | One machine in the cluster. `a100-01` is a node with eight GPUs. | [Nodes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/nodes/) |
| Container image | A packaged filesystem holding a program and everything it needs. Images live in a registry (`ghcr.io`, `quay.io`) and are named `registry/org/name:tag` or `registry/org/name@sha256:<digest>`. A tag can be moved to point at a newer image. A digest names exactly one image forever. | [Images](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/containers/images/) |
| Pod | One running copy of an image (sometimes a few that share a network). It is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs. Every Crucible run is a pod, and so is every agent turn. Pods are disposable: when a pod ends, the files inside it are gone. That is why a task must declare the files it wants kept. | [Pods](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/) |
| Namespace | A named area of a cluster with its own permissions, like a folder. Most `oc` commands take `-n <namespace>` to say which one you mean. | [Namespaces](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/namespaces/) |
| Job | A request to run a pod until it finishes, with a record of whether it succeeded. GPU work in Crucible is submitted as Jobs. | [Jobs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/) |
| Label | A `key=value` tag on a node, pod or Job. Labels are how things are found and grouped. | [Labels](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/labels/) |
| `nodeSelector` | A line in a pod's definition that says "run me only on nodes carrying this label". It is how you ask for a specific GPU model. | [Assigning pods to nodes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/scheduling-eviction/assign-pod-node/) |
| Resource requests and limits | The CPU, memory and GPUs a pod asks for. One GPU is written `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`. A pod that uses more memory than its limit is killed (`OOMKilled`). | [Resource management](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/configuration/manage-resources-containers/), [Scheduling GPUs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-gpus/scheduling-gpus/) |
| Manifest | The YAML text that describes a pod, Job or other object. You hand it to the cluster and the cluster makes it so. | [Kubernetes objects](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/) |
| Kueue | A queue in front of the cluster's GPUs. A Job you submit waits in line until there is quota for it, then starts. Without it, Jobs would race for GPUs. You submit to a LocalQueue (it lives in a namespace). A ClusterQueue behind it holds the quota. While a Job waits or runs, Kueue tracks it as a Workload. | [Kueue overview](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/overview/), [Kueue concepts](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/concepts/) |
| Buildah | A tool that builds a container image from a Containerfile (the same format as a Dockerfile). Crucible's build service, buildit, runs Buildah in pods on the cluster, so you never need Docker on your laptop. | [Buildah](https://buildah.io/), [Containerfile reference](https://github.com/containers/common/blob/main/docs/Containerfile.5.md) |
| Egress | Network traffic leaving a pod. Agent sandboxes block all of it except an allowlist. | [Network policies](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/network-policies/) |

What this means for you in practice: you never write Kubernetes manifests to use Crucible, with one exception. A workflow that runs GPU work submits a Job, and somebody (usually the agent, sometimes a script in your pack) has to write that Job. The Running on pirate tab has an annotated example.

# Access

Get all of these before you start. Each row says what breaks without it.

| You need | How to get it | Without it |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Red Hat VPN | Standard | Nothing resolves. |
| Red Hat SSO login to the web UI | Sign in once | No API key, no desktop sign-in. |
| Rover group `tibrahim-all` | Ask your manager or a Crucible admin | `/playbooks` is empty, and launches and providers are refused. |
| Membership in the `neuralmagic` GitHub org | Standard for the team | You cannot `oc login` to pirate or pirate 2, or read `neuralmagic/crucible-domains`. |
| GitHub team synced to `nm_engine` on pirate (optional) | Ask a pirate admin | You cannot look at your run's pods on the cluster with `oc`. Everything else still works. |
| Group `crucible-kueue-submitters` on pirate (optional) | Ask a pirate admin | You cannot submit GPU Jobs by hand. Your runs can still submit them. |
| An Apple silicon Mac or Fedora (optional, for the desktop app) | Your own machine | No desktop app. Use the web UI and `crux` instead. |

Group changes take effect on your next browser sign-in to the web UI. API keys carry the groups from the sign-in that minted them. If something you were just granted still returns 403, sign out and back in.

## Three ways to drive Crucible

You will use all three. All three talk to the same controller with the same identity.

| Surface | Use it for | Cannot do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Crucible Playbooks (desktop app) | Day-to-day: launching with a provider and model, watching runs live, reading logs and captured files, rerunning from a failed task, drag-and-drop iteration on a pack, notifications. | Edit pack files (it opens your editor), or publish and graduate drafts. |
| Web UI | Account setup (API keys), browsing playbooks, the in-browser draft editor, approvals, secrets, schedules, webhooks, teams, admin. | Pick a provider or model on the plain launch form (only the draft editor's test fire has the picker). |
| `crux` CLI and the MCP server | Scripting, pushing a pack directory as a draft, launching from a shell, tailing logs, and letting your own coding agent write and launch packs. | Mint API keys, manage teams or policy, or create schedules (it can list them). |

*The desktop app. Playbooks are on the left. The selected run's tasks and log fill the rest.*

# Setup

Do these in order. Budget about 30 minutes.

## Sign in to the web UI

1\. Connect to the VPN.

2\. Open [https\://crucible.apps.int.spoke.prod.us-east-1.aws.paas.redhat.com](https://crucible.apps.int.spoke.prod.us-east-1.aws.paas.redhat.com) and sign in with Red Hat SSO.

3\. Check your name and role in the top right.

4\. Open `/playbooks`. If it is empty, you are not in `tibrahim-all` yet (see the Access tab).

5\. Open `/teams`. You should see the teams you belong to.

## Mint an API key

1\. Open `/settings`.

2\. Name the key after the machine it will live on, keep the 90-day default and mint it.

3\. Copy the `crk_...` value now. It is shown only once. The controller stores only a hash, so a lost key cannot be recovered, only replaced. Revoke old keys on the same page.

Minting is browser-only on purpose, so that a key cannot mint another key.

![][image2]

*The web UI's Settings page. The API keys section is at the bottom: name the key, keep 90 days, click Mint key.*

## Install the desktop app (Crucible Playbooks)

macOS (Apple silicon only):

1\. Download `Crucible-Playbooks-v0.6.4-aarch64-apple-darwin.zip` from [https\://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible/releases/latest](https://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible/releases/latest)

2\. Unzip it into `/Applications`.

3\. It is ad-hoc signed, so clear the quarantine flag once:

`xattr -d com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Crucible Playbooks.app"`

Alternatively, open it once, then go to System Settings \> Privacy & Security and click Open Anyway.

Fedora (x86\_64 or aarch64): each release carries an RPM with the app and `crucible-lsp`.

`v=0.6.4; sudo dnf install "https://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible/releases/download/v$v/crucible-playbooks-$v-1.fc45.$(uname -m).rpm"`

On either system, one command installs the newest release and checks its checksum. On macOS it unpacks into `/Applications`:

`curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neuralmagic/crucible/main/scripts/install-desktop.sh | sh`

First run:

1\. Open the app. With no profile, it tries the `crux` config (see Install the CLIs, below). If that is not set up yet, the sidebar shows Sign in with browser.

2\. Click it. A browser tab opens on the controller. Approve the request there, and the app receives its own 90-day key (revocable on the web UI's `/settings` page). You can also paste a `crk_` key into the "or paste a crk\_ key" field.

3\. The account row at the bottom of the sidebar shows who you are. Hover it for role and endpoint.

Profiles (one per controller) live in `~/.config/crucible-playbooks/config.toml` and are edited under Settings (⌘,) \> Profiles. A profile with `auth = "crux"` shares the key with the `crux` CLI, so signing in once signs in both.

![][image3]

*Settings in the desktop app (⌘,). Each profile is one controller. The account row at the bottom left shows who you are signed in as.*

## Install the CLIs: `crux`, `crucible`, `crucible-lsp`

The release tarball has all three binaries. The download command uses the GitHub CLI (`gh`, [https\://cli.github.com/](https://cli.github.com/)). You can also download the file from the releases page in a browser.

`gh release download v0.6.4 --repo neuralmagic/crucible --pattern 'crucible-v0.6.4-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz'`

`mkdir -p ~/.local/bin && tar xzf crucible-v0.6.4-aarch64-apple-darwin.tar.gz -C ~/.local/bin ./crucible ./crux ./crucible-lsp`

`xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ~/.local/bin/crucible ~/.local/bin/crux ~/.local/bin/crucible-lsp`

On Linux, use `crucible-v0.6.4-x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu.tar.gz` and skip `xattr`. Make sure `~/.local/bin` is on your `PATH`.

To track `main` instead of a release (needs a Rust toolchain):

`cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible.git crux crucible crucible-lsp`

| Binary | What it is for |
| :---- | :---- |
| `crux` | Talks to the controller: drafts, launches, logs, files, secrets. |
| `crucible` | The engine. Locally, it checks a pack, compiles its graph and runs command-only packs on your laptop for free. |
| `crucible-lsp` | Editor diagnostics, completion and hover for `workflow.star` and `crucible.toml`. |

Point `crux` at MPP:

`mkdir -p ~/.config/crux && printf 'url = "%s"\napi_token = "%s"\n' https://crucible-api.apps.int.spoke.prod.us-east-1.aws.paas.redhat.com crk_PASTE_YOURS > ~/.config/crux/config.toml && chmod 600 ~/.config/crux/config.toml`

The `url` is the API hostname (`crucible-api...`), not the browser one. Environment variables `CONTROLLER_URL` and `CONTROLLER_API_TOKEN` override the file.

Check it:

`crux whoami`

You should see `credential: api key`, your SSO username as `user` and a role other than `viewer`. Do not continue until this is right.

`crux playbook-caps`

This prints the per-launch caps (today \$50 and 3h). Every launch must ask for no more than that.

## Hook up your coding agent over MCP (optional, recommended)

The controller serves the same operations as `crux` over [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) (Model Context Protocol, the standard way to give a coding agent extra tools). The command below is for [Claude Code](https://docs.claude.com/en/docs/claude-code/overview). With it hooked up, Claude Code can draft a pack with you, push it, launch it and read the results.

`claude mcp add --transport http crucible https://crucible-api.apps.int.spoke.prod.us-east-1.aws.paas.redhat.com/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer crk_PASTE_YOURS"`

The exact command, with your key filled in, is shown on `/settings` right after you mint. Restart Claude Code and ask it to call `crucible_whoami`.

For agent-written packs, also install the co-draft skill. On `/playbooks/drafts`, use the **Agent skill** download and save the file as `~/.claude/skills/crucible-co-draft/SKILL.md`. It teaches the agent the draft loop (save, read diagnostics, fix, save again) and the version rules.

![][image4]

*The Drafts page in the web UI. The Agent skill download is at the top right.*

## Editor support

* VS Code / Cursor: install `crucible-starlark-v0.6.4.vsix` from the release page (`code --install-extension crucible-starlark-v0.6.4.vsix`). If `crucible-lsp` is not on your `PATH`, point the `crucible.server.path` setting at it.  
* Claude Code: from a checkout of `neuralmagic/crucible`, `just claude-install` adds the `crucible-lsp` plugin. Run `/reload-plugins` in an open session.  
* Neovim, Emacs, Helix, Vim: configs are in `editors/README.md` in the core repo.

The language server activates only in a directory with a `crucible.toml`, or on a file that calls `workflow()`.

## Log in to pirate (optional, for watching pods)

You do not need cluster access to launch or read runs. It helps when you are debugging GPU Jobs and builds.

`oc` is the OpenShift command-line client. Install it first ([https\://docs.okd.io/latest/cli\_reference/openshift\_cli/getting-started-cli.html](https://docs.okd.io/latest/cli_reference/openshift_cli/getting-started-cli.html)):

`brew install openshift-cli`

Then log in. This opens a browser, and the session is saved in `~/.kube/config`:

`oc login --web --server=https://api.openshift.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443`

Pirate signs you in with GitHub (`neuralmagic` org). Your username is your GitHub login. Read access to the Crucible namespaces comes from the `nm_engine` group (see the Access tab).

To check that it worked, list the cluster's machines with the GPU model and CPU architecture of each:

`oc get nodes -L nvidia.com/gpu.product,kubernetes.io/arch`

Pirate 2 has its own login. See the Running on pirate 2 tab.

`oc` commands follow one pattern: `oc -n <namespace> <verb> <kind> <name>`. The verbs you need are `get` (list), `describe` (details and recent events) and `logs` (what a pod printed).

# First launches

These two launches prove your setup end to end before you write anything real. Both packs were run locally while this guide was written.

## Launch 1: a free, command-only pack

Make a directory with exactly these three files. Keep everything else out of the pack directory, because `draft-push` uploads the whole tree.

`hello/crucible.toml`

`[workspace]`  
`inject = ["count.py"]`

`[agent]`  
`backend   = "command"`  
`agent_cmd = "true"`  
`goal      = "Count the words in a fixed sentence."`

`[workflow]`  
`type = "playbook"`  
`file = "workflow.star"`

`hello/workflow.star`

`params = {`  
    `"sentence": {"type": "string", "default": "the quick brown fox", "doc": "text to count"},`  
`}`

`count = command(`  
    `name = "count",`  
    `run = "python3 count.py",`  
    `emits = ["words"],`  
    `emits_files = ["REPORT.md"],`  
`)`

`workflow(type = "playbook", tasks = [count], result = count)`

`hello/count.py`

`import json`  
`import os`  
`from pathlib import Path`

`inputs = json.loads(Path(os.environ["CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE"]).read_text())`  
`sentence = inputs["params"]["sentence"]`  
`words = len(sentence.split())`  
``Path("REPORT.md").write_text(f"# Word count\n\n`{sentence}` has {words} words.\n")``  
`print(json.dumps({"words": str(words)}))`

What each piece does:

* `[workspace] inject` copies `count.py` into the run's workspace. A task can only run files that are injected (or produced by an earlier task).  
* `[agent] backend = "command"` says this pack has no real agent turns. It is the cheapest kind of pack.  
* `params` must be the first statement in `workflow.star`. Each param needs a `default` or `required = True`.  
* `command(...)` runs `sh -c "<run>"` in the workspace. Its result is the last line of stdout, a JSON object with one key per name in `emits`. Values are strings.  
* `emits_files` declares files the task produces. They are captured with the run and handed to downstream tasks.  
* A `command` reads params from the JSON file at `$CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE` under `params`. Params never reach it through `run`.  
* `workflow(...)` lists every task and names the `result` task. A task you build but do not list is a compile error.

Check it locally:

`crucible check --manifest hello/crucible.toml`

`crucible plan compile-workflow --file hello/workflow.star --manifest hello/crucible.toml --param sentence="hello pirate world"`

Run it locally for free. The run writes `workspace/` and `state/` into the directory, so use a copy:

`cp -r hello /tmp/hello-run && cd /tmp/hello-run && crucible plan run --manifest crucible.toml --max-cost 0.10 --max-time 2m --param sentence="hello pirate world"`

You should see `count pass ... out={"words":"3"}` and `verdict: valid`.

Now put it on the controller as a draft. Draft ids are permanent lowercase slugs, so prefix yours with your username.

`crux draft-create jdoe-hello --description "Guide walkthrough"`

`crux draft-push jdoe-hello ./hello --base-version 1`

`crux draft-preview jdoe-hello`

`draft-create` makes version 1 (an empty skeleton). Your first push uses `--base-version 1`. Every later pull or push prints the number the next push must carry. Preview after every push: it compiles what the controller holds and prints diagnostics.

Launch it on pirate:

`crux draft-launch jdoe-hello --dispatch-target pirate --max-cost 1 --max-time 10m --params '{"sentence":"hello pirate world"}'`

`--params` is a JSON object of strings. `--dispatch-target pirate` is the default today, but write it anyway so the launch does not move if the default does.

`draft-launch` prints the launch key and a link. To watch the run:

`crux playbook-runs`

`crux run-log <run_id> -f`

Or open the app, where the run appears at the top of the sidebar. When the run settles, read the report:

`crux run-files <run_id>`

`crux run-file <run_id> count/REPORT.md`

To do the same from the desktop app, drag the `hello` folder onto the Crucible Playbooks Dock icon. The app pushes it as the next version of the draft named after the folder, creating the draft on the first drop. A draft that has never run opens its launch form. After that, a drop test-fires the draft with the target, provider and model of its newest run, under the drop ceilings in Settings (\$1 and 30m by default). Folder drop is macOS only.

![][image5]

*The launch form in the desktop app: params, the Runs on line, and the two ceilings.*

![][image6]

*A finished run. The Tasks pane lists each task with its result, and the Log pane shows what happened in order.*

## Launch 2: add an agent turn

This pack has the same shape, but an agent writes something and a command checks it. The launch costs a small amount of real money.

`hello-agent/crucible.toml`

`[workspace]`  
`inject = ["count.py", "write.md"]`

`[agent]`  
`backend       = "openshell"`  
`harness       = "claude"`  
`sandbox_image = "ghcr.io/neuralmagic/sandbox-triage-cc@sha256:36a11bb264a7268962eaf982986a631e7a2673848b468f8c8fd636c559770333"`  
`goal          = "Write a haiku about a topic, then count its words."`

`[workflow]`  
`type = "playbook"`  
`file = "workflow.star"`

`hello-agent/workflow.star`

`params = {`  
    `"topic": {"type": "string", "default": "a pirate ship made of GPUs", "doc": "what the haiku is about"},`  
`}`

`write = agent(`  
    `name = "write",`  
    `prompt = prompt_file("write.md") + "\n\nTopic: " + param("topic") + "\n",`  
    `emits = ["title"],`  
    `emits_files = ["HAIKU.md"],`  
    `timeout = "10m",`  
`)`

`count = command(`  
    `name = "count",`  
    `run = "python3 count.py",`  
    `depends_on = [write],`  
    `emits = ["words"],`  
    `emits_files = ["REPORT.md"],`  
`)`

`workflow(type = "playbook", tasks = [write, count], result = count)`

`hello-agent/write.md`

`Write a haiku about the topic below.`

``1. Write the haiku to `HAIKU.md` in the workspace root: a `# <title>` line, a blank line, then the three lines.``  
``2. Write `PLAN_TASK_RESULT.json` in the workspace root with exactly one key, `title`, set to the title you chose.``

`Do nothing else: no other files, no network calls.`

`hello-agent/count.py`

`import json`  
`import os`  
`from pathlib import Path`

`inputs = json.loads(Path(os.environ["CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE"]).read_text())`  
`title = inputs["write"]["title"]`  
`haiku = Path("inputs/write/HAIKU.md").read_text()`  
`body = [line for line in haiku.splitlines() if line and not line.startswith("#")]`  
`words = sum(len(line.split()) for line in body)`  
`Path("REPORT.md").write_text(f"# {title}\n\n{len(body)} lines, {words} words.\n\n{haiku}")`  
`print(json.dumps({"words": str(words)}))`

What is new:

* `backend = "openshell"` runs agent turns in a sandbox pod started from `sandbox_image`, a container image that already has the agent CLI and common tools installed. Always pin images by digest (the `@sha256:...` form), because a tag can be repointed and a digest cannot. The Writing workflows tab covers picking one.  
* `agent(prompt = ...)`: params reach an agent only through its prompt. Concatenating `param("topic")` into the prompt is the supported way to pass one.  
* An agent reports its `emits` by writing `PLAN_TASK_RESULT.json`. The agent only knows to do that if the prompt says so and names the file and the exact keys. Forgetting this is the most common first failure: the agent does the work, and then the task fails on a missing field after the money is spent.  
* The command downstream reads the agent's scalar from `$CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE` under the task name (`inputs["write"]["title"]`) and its file from `inputs/write/HAIKU.md`.  
* A task's `timeout` must be no longer than the launch's `--max-time`, or the launch is refused before it starts.

Push the pack, then launch it with a provider and a model. On MPP, always pin both. The `enmaas` provider's default model does not work with the current sandbox images, so a launch without a pin fails its first agent turn at zero tokens.

`crux draft-create jdoe-hello-agent --description "Guide walkthrough, agent turn"`

`crux draft-push jdoe-hello-agent ./hello-agent --base-version 1`

`crux draft-preview jdoe-hello-agent`

`crux draft-launch jdoe-hello-agent --dispatch-target pirate --provider enmaas --model rits/zai-org/glm-5-3 --max-cost 1 --max-time 20m --params '{"topic":"kueue on a friday"}'`

In the desktop app, the **Runs on** line of the launch form has the target pills, the provider picker and the model field. Reruns keep the same choices.

If both launches pass, your setup is complete. Delete the drafts when you are done (`crux draft-delete <id>`).

![][image7]

*Click Change on the Runs on line to pick the target cluster, the provider (Agent) and the model.*

![][image8]

*The Files pane shows what each task captured. Here the agent's one file, next to the pack that produced it.*

# Authoring loop

You will repeat this loop for every pack:

1\. Edit files locally, with `crucible-lsp` in your editor.

2\. Run `crucible check --manifest <dir>/crucible.toml`, then `crucible plan compile-workflow --file <dir>/workflow.star --manifest <dir>/crucible.toml --param k=v` with a `--param` for every required param. `check` reads the manifest and `compile-workflow` compiles the graph. Neither covers the other.

3\. If the pack has no real agent turns, run it locally for free with `crucible plan run`.

4\. Push with `crux draft-push <id> <dir> --base-version <n>`, by dropping the folder on the desktop app, or with Save (⌘S) in the app's draft view.

5\. Preview with `crux draft-preview <id>`. A launch always runs the newest save, so preview what you pushed.

6\. Launch with the smallest ceilings that can finish. Pin target, provider and model.

7\. Read the graph, log and files (see the Debugging runs tab). Fix the pack, then rerun from the failed task instead of from scratch.

Version rules for drafts:

* A push carries the version it was based on. If someone (or your agent) saved in between, the push is refused, not merged. Run `crux draft-pull <id> <newdir>` and reconcile by hand.  
* `draft-push` prints the schema digest. If it matches the skeleton's digest from `draft-create`, you pushed the wrong directory.  
* `crux draft-launch ... --schema-digest <digest from preview>` refuses to run if a save landed after you previewed.

To start from an existing playbook instead of a blank skeleton:

`crux playbooks`

`crux draft-create jdoe-triage --template <playbook id> --description "..."`

`--template` takes a registered playbook id only. For any other draft, run `crux draft-pull <id> ./copy` and copy what you need. In the app, **Draft** on a registered playbook pulls a working copy named `<playbook>-<user>`.

![][image9]

*Draft Studio in the web UI: the pack's files, the compile diagnostics, the resolved sandbox image and a preview of the launch form.*

![][image10]

*The Pack pane in the desktop app shows the same files, with Edit to open them in your editor.*

## Letting your agent write the pack

With the MCP server (see the Setup tab) and the co-draft skill installed, ask Claude Code something like "draft a crucible playbook that ..., using the crucible-co-draft skill". The agent creates the draft, saves the whole pack, reads the `file:line:col` diagnostics, fixes and saves until the pack is clean, then hands you the draft link. Have it launch only when you ask, because launches cost money.

In the desktop app, a failed run or task has a **Fix with agent** button. It copies a brief to your clipboard: what failed, the last log lines, LSP problems, the draft and folder, and the `crux` commands to save a fix and rerun from the failure. Paste it into your agent:

`claude "$(pbpaste)"`

![][image11]

*A failed run. Fix with agent is in the top bar and on the failed task's card.*

# Agent drafting (provisional)

This is not released. It needs a Crucible Playbooks desktop build newer than 0.6.4. The latest release, v0.6.4, and everything older have no Agent pane.

The feature lives on branch `claude/crucible-agent-drafting-1f3ca9` of the core repo. As of 2026-11-11 it is not on main and not in any release, and part of it is uncommitted. It will be in the first release after 0.6.4 once the branch merges. Until then you need a build from that branch.

Expect the steps here to change. Use the Authoring loop tab for anything you need to work today.

## What it is

In the desktop app, a draft's working copy gets an `Agent` button (also ⌘9). It opens an Agent pane that docks, splits and resizes like any other pane. You type what you want changed. A coding agent in a sandbox on your own machine pulls the draft with `crux`, edits it with `crucible-lsp` checking the Starlark, and pushes the next version. It can also preview the draft, launch it and follow the run.

* The agent acts as the user signed in to the app, and as the team you are acting as.  
* When the agent launches a run, the window moves to that run.  
* A prompt sent while a turn is running queues. `Send now` interrupts the turn instead.  
* `Reset` starts a new sandbox. `End` deletes it. The agent remembers earlier prompts only as long as its sandbox lives.

## What you need

| Piece | What it is for |
| :---- | :---- |
| [podman](https://podman.io/) | Runs the sandbox containers |
| [OpenShell](https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell/releases) gateway and CLI, 0.1.5 or newer | Creates sandboxes. The app talks to the gateway |
| A provider on the gateway | Holds the model credential, so the sandbox never sees it |
| The `localhost/crucible-agent` image | The sandbox image: Claude Code, `crux`, `crucible-lsp`, the docs and the draft-a-playbook skill |
| A signed-in profile in the app | The agent works as that user |
| A desktop app build newer than 0.6.4 | Older builds have no Agent pane |

The full guide is `docs/desktop-agent-local.md` on the branch. Read it for exact commands if anything below fails.

## Step 1: podman

`podman machine list`

The machine must be running. Give it at least 8 GiB of memory, because the image build compiles `crux` and `crucible-lsp`.

## Step 2: the OpenShell gateway

Install the `openshell` CLI and `openshell-gateway`, both at the same version, 0.1.5 or newer, and put them on your `PATH`. Then write `~/.config/openshell/gateway.toml`:

`[openshell]`  
`version = 2`

`[openshell.gateway]`  
`bind_address = "0.0.0.0:17670"`  
`compute_driver = "podman"`

Check the file:

`openshell-gateway --config ~/.config/openshell/gateway.toml config preflight`

Start the gateway by hand. It is not a service, so it stops at logout or reboot.

`nohup openshell-gateway --config ~/.config/openshell/gateway.toml >> ~/.local/state/openshell/gateway.log 2>&1 &`

The app uses whichever gateway the `openshell` CLI has active. If this command works, the app can reach the gateway too:

`openshell provider list`

## Step 3: an EnMaaS provider

A provider keeps the model key on the gateway. The sandbox only gets a placeholder, and the gateway swaps in the real key on requests to that provider's host.

1\. Copy `crucible-desktop/sandbox/model-gateway.yaml` from the branch.

2\. In the copy, set `id: enmaas` and `endpoints[0].host: api.enmaas.devshift.net`.

3\. Import it:

`openshell provider profile import -f enmaas.yaml`

4\. Store your EnMaaS key. Put it in the `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` variable for this one command:

`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=<your EnMaaS key> openshell provider create --name enmaas --type enmaas --credential ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`

5\. Point the app at it in `~/.config/crucible-playbooks/config.toml`, then restart the app:

`[agent]`  
`providers = ["enmaas"]`

`[agent.env]`  
`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL = "https://api.enmaas.devshift.net"`

The model defaults to `claude-opus-5-5`. To use another one EnMaaS serves, add a line such as `model = "rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017"` under `[agent]`.

EnMaaS takes the key on `/v1/messages` as an `x-api-key` header. A bearer key gets a 401\. The profile handles this for you.

## Step 4: the sandbox image

From the root of the core repo, on the branch:

`just desktop-agent-image`

This builds `localhost/crucible-agent`. Build it again after a change to `crux`, `crucible-lsp`, `docs/` or `skills/draft-a-playbook`.

## Step 5: use it

1\. Sign in to a controller profile in the app.

2\. Open a playbook's run.

3\. On the Pack pane, press `Draft` or `Edit` to pull a working copy.

4\. Press `Agent` on the working copy's toolbar, or ⌘9.

The first prompt creates the sandbox, which takes a few seconds.

## What was tested

Tested live on 2026-11-11, with Claude Code against EnMaaS:

| Model | Result |
| :---- | :---- |
| `claude-opus-5-5` | Ran a two-prompt session, including a `crux whoami` call through to the controller |
| `rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017` | Same |

With a model that is not Claude, the pane shows a harmless `[claude-code:unrecognized_model]` line each turn. The cost shown per turn is Claude Code's own estimate, not the EnMaaS price.

## Known gaps

* `[agent.env]` is new and only exists in builds from this branch.  
* Setting up the gateway's mTLS certificates on a clean machine is not documented or verified. The tested machine carried them over from an older install.  
* The agent's push, launch and follow path has not been run end to end by a real edit. The sandbox, sign-in, `crux` pull, the LSP and multi-prompt conversation have.

## When it does not work

The pane's status row shows the reason in red.

| What you see | Cause | What to do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `The OpenShell gateway at ... did not answer` | The gateway is not running, or the CLI's active gateway is a different one | Start it (step 2), or run `openshell gateway select <name>` |
| `No OpenShell gateway is registered on this machine` | The CLI has no active gateway | Register the gateway with the CLI |
| `drafting with an agent needs 0.1.5 or newer` | An old gateway binary is running | Install 0.1.5 or newer and restart it |
| Provider not found | The provider named in `[agent]` is not on the gateway | Step 3 |
| The turn ends at once with an auth error | The stored key is wrong or expired | Run the `openshell provider create` command from step 3 again with a good key |
| Every sandbox create fails after a gateway upgrade | Provider profiles written by an older gateway do not decode | Export them on the old version, delete them, and import them on the new one |
| The agent has no memory of the last prompt | The sandbox was replaced (app restart, `Reset`, or the gateway restarted) | Nothing. A session lives as long as its sandbox |

Sandboxes are named `cr-draft-*`. To see what is left over:

`openshell sandbox list`

# Writing workflows

This covers the part of the DSL you will use in your first month. The complete reference is [https\://neuralmagic.github.io/crucible/dsl-reference.html](https://neuralmagic.github.io/crucible/dsl-reference.html) (or `crucible plan dsl-reference`), and the pack format spec is `docs/crucible-contract.md` in the core repo.

## Design rule: commands everywhere, agents only for judgment

If a task can be a script, make it a `command`. Use an agent turn only where judgment is needed (reading code, deciding, editing). Commands are free and reproducible, and they can be trusted to report what happened. A report assembled by an agent cannot. Most good packs have one or two agent turns and end in a `command` that writes the report.

## Task types

| Constructor | Runs | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `command(name, run, ...)` | `sh -c run` in the loop pod (the run's main pod), outside any sandbox | Free. Gets params from `$CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE`. |
| `agent(name, prompt, ...)` | An agent turn in the sandbox | `prompt` is a string. Use `prompt_file("x.md") + ...`. Optional per-task `harness`, `model`, `effort`, `sandbox`, `session`, `repair`. |
| `skill(name, skill, args, ...)` | An agent turn whose instructions are `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` | `args` is how params reach it. |
| `evaluate(name, run, threshold, direction)` | A scoring command | `direction` is `lower` or `higher`. |
| `route(name, questions, ...)` | A branch decided by a task's output, a decision model or a human | See Branches, humans and review loops, below. |
| `report(name, destination={"kind": "slack"}, ...)` | Posts a result |  |

Arguments every task takes: `name`, `depends_on`, `emits`, `emits_files`, `timeout` (`"90s"`, `"10m"`, `"2h"`), `required`, `join`, `isolated`, `over`, `max_fanout`.

## How data moves between tasks

* Scalars (`emits`): a `command` prints a JSON object as its last non-empty stdout line, and an agent writes `PLAN_TASK_RESULT.json`. Send progress to stderr, never to the last stdout line. A missing declared key fails the task, and the task is not retried.  
* Files (`emits_files`): the task writes them in the workspace. Downstream tasks find them, read-only, at `inputs/<task>/<path>`. A missing declared file fails the task, so write it on every code path, including "nothing to do".  
* Inputs to a command: `$CRUCIBLE_INPUTS_FILE` is a JSON file holding each direct dependency's scalars keyed by task name, plus `params`, plus `item` in a fan-out instance. `$CRUCIBLE_INPUTS` holds the same JSON when it is 64 KiB or less.  
* Inputs to an agent: upstream scalars are added to its prompt. Params are not, unless you put them in the prompt.  
* Typed emits: `emits = {"count": "integer", "urls": "links", "verdict": ["ok", "bad"]}` or `schema_file("x.schema.json")`. Use them once the shape matters.  
* Emit locations, not counts. A later task can act on `{file, line, reason}`. It cannot act on `broken = 3`. Counts belong in the final report.

## Params

`params = {`  
    `"repo":  {"type": "string", "required": True, "pattern": "^[A-Za-z0-9-]+/[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$", "doc": "owner/name"},`  
    `"mode":  {"type": "string", "default": "fast", "choices": ["fast", "thorough"]},`  
    `"limit": {"type": "int", "default": 6, "min": 1, "max": 20},`  
    `"dry":   {"type": "bool", "default": True},`  
    `"notes": {"type": "string", "default": "", "multiline": True},`  
`}`

* Types: `string`, `int`, `number`, `bool`, `list<string>`.  
* `choices` and `bool` render as selects in the launch forms.  
* A supplied string param may only flow into a prompt. Putting it in `run`, or calling `str()`, `%`, `.format()` or a string method on it, is a compile error. Int, number and bool params are plain values.  
* That check fires only on supplied values, so a pack can pass `check` with its defaults and then fail when someone launches it with a real value. Always compile with `--param` values.  
* `crucible plan params --file workflow.star` prints the JSON Schema the launch forms use.

## Fan-out, isolation and joins

`check = command(`  
    `name = "check",`  
    `run = "python3 check.py",`  
    `depends_on = [scan],`  
    `over = scan.docs,     # one instance per item in scan's "docs" list`  
    `max_fanout = 20,      # an assertion: a longer list FAILS the task, it does not truncate`  
    `isolated = True,      # own worktree, thrown away; only declared files and scalars survive`  
    `required = False,     # one bad instance does not sink the run`  
    `emits = ["broken"],`  
    `emits_files = ["CHECK.md"],`  
`)`

`roundup = command(name = "roundup", run = "python3 roundup.py", depends_on = [scan, check], join = "passed", ...)`

* An instance reads its item as `inputs["item"]`.  
* Downstream, a fan-out's summary is `{"instances": N, "passed": n, "failed": n, "outputs": {key: {...}}}`. `outputs` lists only passed instances. Its files are at `inputs/check[<key>]/<path>`, with the key interpolated raw (slashes included).  
* Bound the producer so it cannot exceed `max_fanout`. At most 8 instances run at once, and the engine ceiling is 256\.  
* `join = "passed"` consumes only passing instances, `"all"` requires every one, and `"settled"` also stages a failed dependency's files.  
* A required task that depends on an advisory (`required = False`) task with the default join is a compile error. Use `join = "passed"`.

## Sandbox images and harnesses

* Images are built from `images/matrix.toml` in `crucible-domains`: `sandbox-<toolchain>-cc` runs Claude Code, `-codex` runs Codex, `-opencode` and `-pi` run those harnesses. Toolchains include `go`, `rust`, `vllm-<ver>`, `triage` and `omnibus`. Every image has `git`, `gh`, `jq`, `python3` and `uv`.  
* Pin by digest. A tag moves, and a digest is what you tested. To find the digest behind `latest`:

`gh api orgs/neuralmagic/packages/container/sandbox-go-cc/versions --jq '.[] | select(.metadata.container.tags | index("latest")) | .name'`

* Instead of pinning blindly, declare what the turn needs and let the draft editor's image picker choose: `[agent.requires] "toolchain.go" = ">=1.25"`. `requires` refuses a launch on an image that does not satisfy it, while `prefers` only ranks.  
* The image must contain the provider's harness. `enmaas` drives `claude`, `enmaas-opencode` drives `opencode`, and the `openai*` providers drive `codex`, `opencode` or `pi`. A mismatch fails in the first turn.  
* Command tasks do not run in the sandbox image. They run in the loop pod, which has `python3` (stdlib only), `gh`, `jq`, `curl`, `git` and the `buildit` CLI. It has no `uv` and no `pip`. Write command scripts against the standard library.

## Sandbox egress and binaries

The agent sandbox denies egress (outbound network traffic) by default. The built-in allowlist covers the forges, PyPI, the model endpoints and the agent CLIs. To widen it:

`[agent.openshell]`  
`binaries  = ["/usr/bin/git", "/usr/lib/git-core/git-remote-https", "/usr/bin/gh"]`  
`endpoints = ["huggingface.co:443:read-only"]`

`binaries` is the allowlist of executables the agent may run beyond its harness. If the agent says a tool "is not permitted", add its absolute path. `crucible check --manifest crucible.toml` lists the egress and binaries a pack resolves to, and `crucible plan exposure --manifest crucible.toml` prints its output bounds and capability disclosure as JSON.

## Branches, humans and review loops

* `route(...)` branches the graph. Each route has exactly one decider: `source = task` (a task's output, free), `min_confidence = 0.8` (a decision model), or `human = True` (answered in the controller UI, with `review = "template.md"` and `timeout`). Every answer, including `uncertain`, must be covered by a `when`, `otherwise` or `drop`. See `examples/route` and `examples/human-gate`.  
* `revise = <reviewer task>, max_rounds = 2..5` on an agent gives you an author and reviewer loop. See `examples/revise-loop`.  
* `optional(task)` in `depends_on` allows for a branch that is not taken.

## Secrets

Never put a credential in a pack. Declare it, store the value in the registry and bind it to your draft.

`[[secret]]`  
`name = "my-gh-token"`  
`kind = "opaque"        # opaque | file | registry_authfile | kubeconfig`  
`env  = "GH_TOKEN"      # or path = "/abs/path"`

1\. Create the value on the web UI's `/secrets` page (or run `crux secret-create my-gh-token --kind opaque` with the value on stdin).

2\. Bind it to the draft:

`crux secrets`

`crux secret-bind <secret id> --playbook jdoe-mypack --env GH_TOKEN --declared-name my-gh-token`

Visibility is set on the registry entry: `broker_only` (the default: the machinery uses the secret on the agent's behalf) or `agent_visible` (the agent runs `gh` or `git push` itself). Command tasks see both kinds. A pack with an unbound secret previews without errors but is refused at launch.

## Other manifest knobs worth knowing

| Key | What it does |
| :---- | :---- |
| `[agent.resources] gpus, cpu, memory, node_selector` | CPU, memory and GPUs for the agent sandbox pod (not for Kueue Jobs). `node_selector` restricts which nodes it may run on. |
| `[dispatch] target = "pirate"` | Pins every launch of the pack to a cluster. A launch naming another target is refused. Use it when the pack only works on pirate (anything that needs buildit or Kueue, which pirate 2 lacks). |
| `[agent.overrides] allow = ["model"]` | Lets a launch override per-task harness/model/effort with `--param '*.model=X'`. Without it, nothing can be overridden per task. |
| `[agent.sandbox.<name>]` | A second sandbox image for some tasks. Select it with `agent(..., sandbox = "<name>")`. |
| `[[agent.relay]]` | Files rendered host-side into the sandbox (config and credentials files) that never live in the repo. |
| `edition = 2` with `[workflow] env = ["NAME?"]` | Command tasks get only a minimal environment plus what you list. Recommended for new packs. |
| `[repo] url, ref` | Starts the workspace from a clone. Without it the workspace starts with only your injects. Most playbooks clone inside a task from a param. |
| `[workspace] inject` | Strings are frozen copies, restored before every task so an agent cannot edit the script that checks it. `{src, dst, frozen = false}` is a one-time fixture. Globs and directories work. |

# Running on pirate

## How your launch gets there

* MPP is the hub: the cluster where the controller runs. Pirate is a spoke: a second cluster the controller starts pods on. Pirate is the default dispatch target today.  
* Pirate 2 is a second spoke (`--dispatch-target pirate2`) with B200 GPUs and no build or GPU queue services. It has its own tab, Running on pirate 2\. Everything on this tab is about pirate.  
* Choose it explicitly with `--dispatch-target pirate` in `crux`, the Runs on target pill in the desktop app, the `dispatch_target` field on a schedule or watch, or `[dispatch] target = "pirate"` in the pack.  
* The web UI launch form hides the target picker when only one target is offered to you.  
* Every pod of a launch lands on the same cluster.

## What runs where on pirate

A run's pods are spread over four namespaces. You need the names only to look at things with `oc`.

| Namespace | What lives there |
| :---- | :---- |
| `crucible-system` | Your run's loop pod `crucible-run-<name>` (engine plus command tasks), the run's `buildit` MCP, the shared `buildit-cache`, the `crucible-kueue` servers. |
| `crucible-sandboxes` | Agent sandbox pods and each run's OpenShell gateway (the proxy that enforces the sandbox's network allowlist). |
| `crucible-builds` | buildit builder pods, one per image build. Kueue queue `builds`, no GPUs. |
| `crucible-kueue-e2e` | GPU Jobs your run submits. They wait in the Kueue LocalQueue `crucible-e2e`. |

## Hardware

Pirate has 13 nodes (machines), surveyed on 2026-11-11. Each row is a group of nodes. The label in the last column is what a `nodeSelector` matches.

| Nodes | CPU and memory | GPUs | `nvidia.com/gpu.product` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| a100-01, 02, 03, 04, 06, 07, 08 (Supermicro AS-4124GO-NART) | 256 CPUs and about 2 TiB of memory each (AMD) | 8x A100 each (a100-06 has 7), 80 GB of GPU memory per card, 55 total | `NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB` |
| b200-02, dgx-b200-1 (NVIDIA DGX B200) | 224 CPUs and about 2 TiB of memory each (Intel) | 8x B200 each, 183 GB per card, 16 total | `NVIDIA-B200` |
| master0, master1, master2 | 256 CPUs and about 500 GiB of memory each (AMD) | None |  |
| cpu-07 | 80 CPUs and 251 GiB of memory (arm64) | None |  |

Other facts worth knowing:

* There is no a100-05, and pirate has no H100s.  
* cpu-07 is the only arm64 node. Everything else is x86\_64. An image built for one architecture does not run on the other.  
* The three master nodes are the control plane (the machines that run Kubernetes itself) and also accept ordinary pods. Loop pods and builds usually land there or on cpu-07.  
* GPUs are whole cards. There is no time-slicing or MPS, so `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` is one full card.  
* The GPU nodes have InfiniBand RDMA networking, offered to pods as the resource `rdma/rdma_shared_device_ib`. Multi-node work uses it. A single-GPU job does not need it.  
* No node is tainted, so nothing stops a pod from landing on a GPU node except what it asks for.  
* The NVIDIA driver is 595.71.05. OpenShift is 4.22.18 (Kubernetes 1.35).

Kueue's quota for Crucible GPU Jobs:

| ClusterQueue | LocalQueue your run submits to | GPU quota | Steers to a GPU model? |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `crucible` | `crucible-e2e` in `crucible-kueue-e2e` | 47 GPUs | No. Its GPU flavor carries no node labels. |
| `crucible-b200` | (measurement queues in other namespaces) | 16 GPUs | Yes, to `NVIDIA-B200`. |

The `crucible` queue does not pick a GPU model for you, so a GPU Job with no `nodeSelector` can land on a B200 node. Always set a `nodeSelector` on `nvidia.com/gpu.product` in GPU Jobs. The Job example below shows where it goes. The quota is shared with other teams' queues, so a Job can wait even when your own run has submitted nothing else.

## Storage

A pod's own files vanish when it ends. To keep data across pods (a model cache, for example) a pod claims a volume, which is a piece of disk the cluster hands out. A [storage class](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes/) is the kind of disk you ask for, and a [PersistentVolumeClaim](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/) (PVC) is the request. The access mode says who can mount it: `ReadWriteOnce` (RWO) is one node at a time, `ReadWriteMany` (RWX) is many pods on many nodes.

| Storage class | Backed by | Access | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `lvms-a100-tier1-storage` | Local NVMe on each A100 node. 1.3 to 13 TiB free per node on 2026-11-11. | RWO | Fast. The volume lives on one node and pins its pods there. Use it for a model cache next to a GPU. |
| `lvms-b200-gpu-ib-tier1-storage` | Local NVMe on the two B200 nodes. 3.1 and 13 TiB free. | RWO | Same, for B200 work. |
| `lvms-control-plane-storage` (the default) | Local NVMe on the master nodes | RWO | A PVC that names no storage class gets this one, and its pod can then only run on a master node, which has no GPU. Always name a class. |
| `nfs` | An in-cluster NFS server | RWX or RWO | Shared across nodes. The class most people use for shared scratch. |
| `nfs-rdma`, `nfs-h100-tcp` | An external NFS filer (NFS 4.2) | RWX | Shared across nodes. Data is kept when the PVC is deleted. |

The three `lvms-` classes are local disk ([LVM Storage](https://docs.okd.io/latest/storage/persistent_storage/persistent_storage_local/persistent-storage-using-lvms.html)). A volume there is deleted with its PVC, and nothing is backed up.

Crucible already uses storage on your behalf, so most workflows never create a PVC:

* The shared build cache (`buildit-cache`) makes repeat image builds fast.  
* Each agent sandbox gets a 2 GiB workspace volume from the default storage class. It is deleted with the sandbox. Because the default class lives on the master nodes, this is what stops a sandbox from being pinned to a GPU node today (see Giving the agent sandbox a GPU, below).  
* Files reach later tasks through `capture`, not through volumes.

The storage classes matter when a Job you submit needs a model cache that outlives it. Create the PVC once by hand, on the class that matches the GPU nodes you select, and mount it in the Job.

## What your run is given: `buildit` and `kueue`

Every run on pirate gets two MCP servers (sets of tools) that its agent can call, and the loop pod has the `buildit` CLI for command tasks. Between them, a workflow can build a container image and run it on a GPU without anyone touching the cluster by hand. Do not declare them in the pack: your own `[mcp.buildit]` clashes by name and breaks every turn.

* buildit builds container images on the cluster with [Buildah](https://buildah.io/), from a Containerfile (the same format as a Dockerfile) in the workspace. Its tools are `build`, `run`, `push`, `status`, `logs` and `clean`. Builder pods run in `crucible-builds` and share a compiler cache ([ccache](https://ccache.dev/)), so the second vLLM build is much faster than the first. A build is capped at 1 hour and a `run` at 30 minutes.  
* kueue submits GPU work to [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/overview/) and watches it. Its tools are `whoami`, `queues_list`, `queue_describe`, `hardware_describe`, `workload_plan`, `workload_submit`, `workload_status`, `workload_logs`, `workload_stop` and `workload_delete`. Runs can submit to the queue `crucible-e2e` in the namespace `crucible-kueue-e2e`. A plain [Job](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/job/) covers most needs. It also accepts [RayJob](https://docs.ray.io/en/latest/cluster/kubernetes/getting-started/rayjob-quick-start.html), [LeaderWorkerSet](https://lws.sigs.k8s.io/), [Deployment](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/deployment/) and [StatefulSet](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/statefulset/).

Jobs are labelled with `crucible.dev/run-id`, so you can find your run's work with `oc`.

The Builds and GPU Jobs tab shows how to use both from a pack, step by step, with a worked example.

## What a GPU Job looks like

If you have never seen a Kubernetes manifest, this is the whole of one. The agent normally writes it and submits it through the kueue server, but you will read these when a Job misbehaves.

`apiVersion: batch/v1`  
`kind: Job`  
`metadata:`  
  `generateName: moe-bench-`  
  `namespace: crucible-kueue-e2e`  
  `labels:`  
    `kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name: crucible-e2e`  
`spec:`  
  `backoffLimit: 0`  
  `template:`  
    `spec:`  
      `restartPolicy: Never`  
      `nodeSelector:`  
        `nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB`  
      `containers:`  
        `- name: bench`  
          `image: quay.io/wseaton/crucible-smoke@sha256:<digest>`  
          `command: ["python3", "bench.py"]`  
          `resources:`  
            `limits:`  
              `nvidia.com/gpu: 1`

Line by line:

* `kind: Job` asks for a pod that runs once to completion.  
* `generateName` gives every submission a fresh name (`moe-bench-x7k2p`), so two Jobs never collide.  
* `namespace` is where the Job lives. Runs may only submit to `crucible-kueue-e2e`.  
* The `kueue.x-k8s.io/queue-name` label puts the Job in a Kueue queue. Without it, Kueue does not manage the Job. See [Running a Job with Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/tasks/run/jobs/).  
* `backoffLimit: 0` and `restartPolicy: Never` mean a failed Job stays failed and is not retried. You want that for a measurement.  
* `nodeSelector` pins the Job to A100 nodes.  
* `image` is the container to run, pinned by digest.  
* `command` is what runs inside it. The Job succeeds if this exits 0\.  
* `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` asks for one GPU. The Job waits in the queue until one is free.

Whatever the command prints is the Job's log. A pod's files vanish when it ends, so print the result (the hill climb prints one JSON line) and have the submitting task read it from the log.

## Giving the agent sandbox a GPU

A Job is the right shape for a measurement: it runs one command and ends. Sometimes the agent itself needs a GPU, to load a model and poke at it, or to profile and retry in one turn. For that, ask for a GPU on the sandbox pod in `crucible.toml`:

`[agent]`  
`backend       = "openshell"`  
`sandbox_image = "ghcr.io/neuralmagic/<image>@sha256:<digest>"`

`[agent.resources]`  
`gpus          = 1`  
`cpu           = "4"`  
`memory        = "16Gi"`  
`node_selector = { "nvidia.com/gpu.product" = "NVIDIA-RTX-PRO-6000-Blackwell-Server-Edition" }`

What each line does:

* `gpus` is the number of whole GPUs the sandbox pod gets (`nvidia.com/gpu` in Kubernetes terms).  
* `cpu` and `memory` are Kubernetes quantities. The pod is guaranteed that much and cannot use more. A process that goes over the memory figure is killed.  
* `node_selector` picks the nodes by label, exactly as in a Job.

Inside the sandbox, the GPU shows up the usual way: `nvidia-smi` works and CUDA sees device 0\. The cluster supplies the driver. The sandbox image has to supply everything else (PyTorch, vLLM, your tools), so pick or build an image that has them.

Where it works today (tested 2026-11-11 with the draft `gpu-sandbox-smoke`):

| Cluster | `node_selector` value | Result |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| pirate 2 | `NVIDIA-RTX-PRO-6000-Blackwell-Server-Edition` | Works. The agent's `nvidia-smi` reported the card, 97887 MiB. |
| pirate 2 | `NVIDIA-B200` | Does not start. The sandbox pod stays `Pending` and the task fails after about five minutes. |
| pirate | `NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB` or `NVIDIA-B200` | Not tested. Expected to fail the same way. |

The reason is storage, not GPUs. Every sandbox gets a small workspace volume (2 GiB) from the cluster's default storage class. On pirate 2 that class only exists on the node with the RTX PRO 6000, so a sandbox pinned to a B200 node has nowhere to put its workspace. On pirate the default class lives on the master nodes, which have no GPUs. Until the deployment gives sandboxes a workspace class that exists on the GPU nodes, the RTX PRO 6000 on pirate 2 is the one GPU a sandbox can hold. If you need an A100 or a B200, run the work as a Kueue Job instead.

Things to know before you use it:

* The table applies to every agent and skill turn in the pack. A fan-out of four turns asks for four GPUs at once, and pirate 2 has one RTX PRO 6000\.  
* It only works with `backend = "openshell"`. The engine refuses the table on any other backend.  
* Sandbox GPUs do not go through Kueue. The pod takes a free GPU directly, or waits as `Pending` until one is free, and nothing counts it against a quota. The GPU is held for the whole turn, including the time the agent spends thinking. Keep the turn short and prefer a Job for anything long.  
* Always set `node_selector`. Without it the sandbox takes whichever GPU model is free.

To check from inside a turn, have the agent run `nvidia-smi` first and stop if it fails. The sandbox pod is in `crucible-sandboxes`, and `oc describe pod` on it shows the GPU under Limits and, when it is stuck, the reason under Events.

## Providers that work from pirate

Pin provider and model on every launch.

| Use | Provider | Model |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| General agent work, cheap | `enmaas` | `rits/zai-org/glm-5-3` |
| Long code-editing loops (what the hill-climb uses) | `enmaas` | `rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017` |
| The strongest Claude, when cost matters less | `vertex` | `claude-opus-4-6` |
| opencode harness on GLM | `enmaas-opencode` | `rits/zai-org/glm-5-3` (needs an `-opencode` image) |

`crux providers` lists what you can use. GLM is text-only. An image anywhere in the conversation gets every later request rejected, so never hand screenshots to an agent running on it.

## Network notes

* Pirate is on the internal network. It reaches internal mirrors (for example `rhsm-pulp.corp.redhat.com`) that other clusters cannot, which is why Red Hat image builds go there.  
* buildit pushes to `quay.io/wseaton/crucible-smoke` and to the internal registry `image-registry.openshift-image-registry.svc:5000/crucible-builds/buildit`. Kueue Jobs pull pushed candidates from quay.  
* Builder pods can reach any host on TCP 443 (HTTPS), plus the cache and the internal registry. Nothing else.

## Watching your run on the cluster

Get the run name from `crux playbook-run <key>` or the app's run header, then:

The run's main pod, with the node it landed on (`-o wide` adds the node column):

`oc -n crucible-system get pod crucible-run-<name> -o wide`

Its agent sandbox pods:

`oc -n crucible-sandboxes get pods | grep <name>`

The GPU Jobs it submitted, their Kueue Workloads and their pods (`-l` filters by label):

`oc -n crucible-kueue-e2e get jobs,workloads,pods -o wide -l crucible.dev/run-id=crucible-run-<name>`

What one Job printed:

`oc -n crucible-kueue-e2e logs job/<job>`

Why a pod is stuck (the Events at the bottom of the output say what the cluster is waiting for):

`oc -n crucible-kueue-e2e describe pod <pod>`

How busy the queues are:

`oc get localqueues -A && oc get clusterqueues`

Statuses you will see in the `STATUS` column, and what they mean:

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `Pending` | The pod is waiting for a node, or (for a Job) for its turn in the Kueue queue. | Usually nothing. If it lasts, check the queue. |
| `ContainerCreating` | The node is pulling the image. A 20 GB vLLM image takes minutes on a node that has never pulled it. | Wait. |
| `Running` | The program is running. | Read its logs. |
| `Completed` | The program exited 0\. | Nothing. |
| `Error` | The program exited non-zero. | Read its logs. |
| `ImagePullBackOff` | The image name or digest is wrong, or the registry refused the pull. | Check the image reference. |
| `OOMKilled` | The pod used more memory than its limit. | Raise the limit or use less memory. |

A Kueue Workload has its own state: not admitted (waiting for quota), admitted (running) or finished.

Read access lets you list things and read logs. It does not let you open a shell in a pod (`oc exec`) or read secrets.

# Running on pirate 2

Pirate 2 is a second spoke, added on 2026-11-09. It is a smaller, newer cluster with B200 GPUs and fast local disks. It runs command tasks and sandboxed agent turns. It does not have the build and GPU queue services that pirate has, so check the comparison below before you move a pack there.

## How to target it

The dispatch target name is `pirate2`. Everything else about a launch is the same.

`crux draft-launch jdoe-hello --dispatch-target pirate2 --max-cost 1 --max-time 10m --params '{"sentence":"hello pirate two"}'`

In the desktop app, pick the pirate2 pill on the Runs on line. To pin a pack to it, set `[dispatch] target = "pirate2"` in `crucible.toml`. `pirate` stays the default when you name no target.

## Pirate and pirate 2 side by side

|  | pirate | pirate 2 |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Dispatch target | `pirate` (default) | `pirate2` |
| Cluster API | [https\://api.openshift.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443](https://api.openshift.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443) | [https\://api.pirate2.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443](https://api.pirate2.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443) |
| Web console | [https\://console-openshift-console.apps.openshift.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com](https://console-openshift-console.apps.openshift.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com) | [https\://console-openshift-console.apps.pirate2.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com](https://console-openshift-console.apps.pirate2.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com) |
| Command tasks | Yes | Yes |
| Sandboxed agent turns | Yes | Yes |
| buildit (image builds) | Yes | No |
| kueue server and Kueue queues | Yes | No. Kueue is not installed. |
| Per-run git proxy | Yes | No |
| GPUs | 55x A100 80 GB, 16x B200 | 16x B200, 1x RTX PRO 6000 |
| GPU in the agent sandbox (`[agent.resources]`) | Not today (untested, expected to fail) | RTX PRO 6000 only (tested) |
| Shared (RWX) storage | Yes, NFS | No, local disk only |
| arm64 node | cpu-07 | None |
| Namespaces a run uses | `crucible-system`, `crucible-sandboxes`, `crucible-builds`, `crucible-kueue-e2e` | `crucible-system`, `crucible-sandboxes` |

What that means for a pack:

* A pack of command tasks and agent turns runs on pirate 2 unchanged.  
* A pack that calls `buildit` or the kueue tools fails on pirate 2, because neither server is there. The vLLM hill climb is one of these. Keep it on pirate.  
* A pack whose agent needs a GPU directly can run on pirate 2 with `[agent.resources]`, on the one RTX PRO 6000\. The B200s there are not reachable from a run yet.  
* A pack whose agent pushes through the per-run git proxy needs pirate.

## Hardware

Pirate 2 has six nodes, all x86\_64. The label in the last column is what a `nodeSelector` matches.

| Nodes | CPU and memory | GPUs | `nvidia.com/gpu.product` |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| dell-b200-01, dell-b200-02 (Dell PowerEdge XE9680L) | 224 CPUs and about 2 TiB of memory each (Intel) | 8x B200 each, 183 GB of GPU memory per card, 16 total | `NVIDIA-B200` |
| lenovo-sr675v3-01 (Lenovo ThinkSystem SR675 V3) | 512 CPUs and about 1.5 TiB of memory (AMD) | 1x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 96 GB | `NVIDIA-RTX-PRO-6000-Blackwell-Server-Edition` |
| cpu-03, cpu-05, cpu-09 | 112 to 160 CPUs and 377 to 503 GiB of memory each (Intel) | None |  |

Other facts worth knowing:

* The three cpu nodes are the control plane (the machines that run Kubernetes itself) and also accept ordinary pods.  
* The B200 nodes have RDMA networking (RoCE): ten fast network interfaces per node, each offered to pods as two virtual functions under resource names like `roce/ens31f0np0_vf`. Multi-node training and inference use these. A single-GPU job does not need them.  
* GPUs are whole cards. There is no time-slicing or MPS, so `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` is one full B200.  
* The NVIDIA driver is 615.71.09. OpenShift is 4.22.9 (Kubernetes 1.35).  
* Nothing queues GPU work here. A pod that asks for a GPU either starts at once or stays `Pending` until one is free.  
* A run gets a GPU on pirate 2 by asking for one on the agent sandbox. Today that works for the RTX PRO 6000 only, not for the B200s. See Giving the agent sandbox a GPU on the Running on pirate tab for the reason and the settings.

## Storage

A pod's own files vanish when it ends. To keep data across pods (a model cache, for example) a pod claims a volume, which is a piece of disk the cluster hands out. A [storage class](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/storage-classes/) is the kind of disk you ask for, and a [PersistentVolumeClaim](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/storage/persistent-volumes/) (PVC) is the request.

| Storage class | Backed by | Free space (2026-11-09) | Notes |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `lvms-b200-tier1-storage` | Local NVMe on the two B200 nodes | About 7.0 TiB on dell-b200-01, 6.5 TiB on dell-b200-02 | Use this for anything that runs on a B200 node. |
| `lvms-gtx-tier1-storage` (the default) | Local NVMe on lenovo-sr675v3-01 | About 1.8 TiB | A PVC that names no storage class gets this one, and its pod can then only run on the Lenovo node. |

Both classes are local disk ([LVM Storage](https://docs.okd.io/latest/storage/persistent_storage/persistent_storage_local/persistent-storage-using-lvms.html), formatted XFS), which has three consequences:

* A volume lives on one node. Any pod that mounts it is pinned to that node.  
* Volumes are `ReadWriteOnce`: one node at a time. There is no shared filesystem class.  
* The volume is deleted when its PVC is deleted. Nothing here is a backup.

The cluster also has an S3 driver (Mountpoint for Amazon S3) that a few teams use to mount buckets read-write-many. It has no storage class, so an admin sets up each mount by hand.

Crucible uses one piece of this. Each agent sandbox gets a 2 GiB workspace volume from the default storage class, deleted with the sandbox. The default class exists only on the Lenovo node, so sandboxes run there. Files reach later tasks through `capture`, not through volumes. The other storage class matters when you run your own pods next to a run.

## Access and watching

Log in the same way as pirate, with your GitHub login:

`oc login --web --server=https://api.pirate2.nm.rdu4.corp.redhat.com:6443`

`oc` remembers one login per cluster and talks to whichever you logged in to last. `oc config get-contexts` lists them, and `oc config use-context <name>` switches.

The loop pod and sandbox pods are in the same namespaces as on pirate:

`oc -n crucible-system get pod crucible-run-<name> -o wide`

`oc -n crucible-sandboxes get pods | grep <name>`

As of 2026-11-09 no team group has been granted read access to these two namespaces on pirate 2, so unless you are a cluster admin these commands are refused. The web UI, the desktop app and `crux` show the same logs without any cluster access.

Providers behave as on pirate: pin `enmaas` to a model, and Vertex works. Pirate 2 is on the same internal network as pirate.

# Builds and GPU Jobs

Most GPU workflows have the same three steps: build a container image, run it on a GPU, check what it printed. Crucible gives a run two services for the first two steps. This tab is the how-to. Both services exist on pirate only.

| Service | What it does | From a `command` or `evaluate` task | From an agent turn |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| buildit | Builds a container image on the cluster with [Buildah](https://buildah.io/) and pushes it to a registry | Yes, through the `buildit` command | Yes, through the buildit tools |
| kueue | Submits a GPU Job to [Kueue](https://kueue.sigs.k8s.io/docs/overview/), waits for it and reads its log | Yes since v0.6.2, through the `crucible_kueue` Python package | Yes, through the kueue tools |

Neither step needs judgment, so both belong in `command` tasks, where they cost nothing and behave the same every time. Before v0.6.2 only an agent could reach kueue, so older packs use a thin agent turn for the run step. Both ways are shown below.

## The standard shape

`build    command   buildit builds the image and pushes it. Emits the image reference.`  
   `|`  
`run      command   Submits one Job through kueue, waits, keeps its log. (Older packs: a thin agent turn.)`  
   `|`  
`verify   evaluate  Reads the file, pulls out the numbers, passes or fails the run.`

If you do use an agent for the run step, keep its part thin. Its prompt is a fixed recipe ("submit exactly this Job, wait, copy the replies into a file"), not an open question. Either way the numbers come from the Job's log, read by a script, so nothing depends on a model summarizing correctly.

## Step 1: build an image with buildit

Put everything the build needs in one directory of the pack (the build context) and tell Crucible to copy it into the run's workspace:

`[workspace]`  
`inject = ["image"]`

buildit builds in one of two ways.

| Way | Command | Use it when |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Containerfile | `buildit build -c image` | `image/` has a Containerfile (the same format as a Dockerfile). This is the general case. |
| Base plus one layer | `buildit build -c image --base <image> --script "sh /opt/x/build.sh" --path /opt/x` | You are adding to a very large base image, such as a vLLM release. buildit copies the context to `--path` inside the base image, runs `--script` there, and saves `--path` as one new layer. The base is never unpacked or pushed again, so the build and every later pull are fast. |

Flags you will use:

| Flag | Meaning |
| :---- | :---- |
| `-c <dir>` | The build context, a directory inside the workspace. |
| `--build-arg KEY=VALUE` | A value for the build. In base-plus-layer mode the script sees it as an environment variable. Repeatable. |
| `--ccache` | Point the compiler cache ([ccache](https://ccache.dev/)) at the cluster's shared cache, so C++ and CUDA code compiled once is not compiled again. |
| `--timeout <seconds>` | Stop the build after this long. |
| `--target <stage>` | Build one stage of a multi-stage Containerfile. |
| `--no-wait` | Return at once instead of waiting for the build to end. |

What comes back:

* `buildit build` waits for the build, then prints one JSON object on standard output. The fields you need are `build_id`, `status` (`succeeded`, `failed` or `cancelled`), `timed_out` and `log_tail` (the end of the build log).  
* It exits non-zero when the build did not succeed, so a failed build fails the task.  
* `buildit push <build_id>` copies a succeeded build to the registry the cluster is set up to publish to, and prints `{"image": "<repository>@sha256:<digest>"}`. That digest reference is what the GPU Job pulls. You do not choose the repository.

A complete build task:

`build = command(`  
    `name = "build",`  
    `run = r"""set -eu`  
`mkdir -p results`  
`if ! buildit build -c image --timeout 3600 > results/status.json 2> results/buildit.log; then`  
    `jq -r '.log_tail // .error' results/status.json | tail -c 1500 >&2`  
    `exit 1`  
`fi`  
`buildit push "$(jq -r .build_id results/status.json)" > results/build.json`  
`cat results/build.json""",`  
    `timeout = "75m",`  
    `emits = {"image": "string"},`  
    `emits_files = ["results/build.json"],`  
`)`

Line by line:

* `buildit build ... > results/status.json` keeps the JSON reply. The `2>` part keeps buildit's progress messages out of the task's result.  
* On failure, the `jq` line prints the end of the build log. Crucible shows only the start of a failed task's error output, and the cause of a failed build is at the end of its log.  
* `buildit push` writes `results/build.json`, and `cat` prints it as the last line, which makes `image` the task's result (see How data moves between tasks on the Writing workflows tab).  
* `emits_files` keeps `results/build.json` so the next task can read it at `inputs/build/results/build.json`.

Other buildit commands, all taking a `build_id`:

| Command | What it does |
| :---- | :---- |
| `buildit status <id>` | The state of a build started with `--no-wait`. |
| `buildit logs <id>` | The build log. It can search (`grep`) or show the last lines. |
| `buildit run <id> --fetch /out -- <command>` | Run a command in a fresh pod of the built image and copy `/out` back to `.buildit/<id>/` in the workspace. Good for a quick test that needs no GPU. |
| `buildit clean` | Delete this run's builds. |

Things that trip people up:

* Builder pods reach the network over HTTPS (port 443\) only. A build step that downloads over plain `http://` (older `apt` sources, for example) hangs or fails. Rewrite the URLs to `https://` in the build script.  
* The context must be inside the workspace. A task with `isolated = True` runs in its own copy of the workspace, and buildit refuses a context from there. Build from a task that is not isolated.  
* The first build of a large project is slow (the first vLLM source build took most of an hour). Later builds with `--ccache` are much faster.

An agent can build too. It has the same operations as tools (`build`, `status`, `logs`, `run`, `push`, `clean`) and the context is a directory of its sandbox workspace. The one difference: the `build` tool returns a `build_id` at once, and the agent calls `status` until the build ends. Let an agent build only when the build is part of what it is deciding, as in the hill climb, where it edits code and rebuilds in a loop.

## Step 2 without an agent: kueue from a command task

Since v0.6.2 a `command` or `evaluate` task can call kueue itself, so the run step needs no agent turn and no model. This is the cheaper and more repeatable way, and new packs should start here. Lucas's pack below was written before it existed, which is why it uses agents.

Name the server in `crucible.toml`:

`[workflow]`  
`type    = "playbook"`  
`file    = "workflow.star"`  
`servers = ["kueue"]`

Then call it from Python with the `crucible_kueue` package, which the loop image ships:

`import asyncio, json`  
`from crucible_kueue import AsyncClient`

`JOB = {`  
    `"apiVersion": "batch/v1",`  
    `"kind": "Job",`  
    `"metadata": {"name": "bench-" + RUN_SUFFIX},`  
    `"spec": {"backoffLimit": 0, "template": {"spec": {`  
        `"restartPolicy": "Never",`  
        `"nodeSelector": {"nvidia.com/gpu.product": "NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB"},`  
        `"containers": [{`  
            `"name": "main",`  
            `"image": IMAGE,`  
            `"command": ["sh", "/opt/x/run.sh"],`  
            `"resources": {"limits": {"nvidia.com/gpu": "1"}},`  
        `}],`  
    `}}},`  
`}`

`async def main():`  
    `kueue = AsyncClient()`  
    `log = await kueue.run("crucible-e2e", JOB, timeout=3600, grep="result ")`  
    `print(json.dumps({"log": log}))`

`asyncio.run(main())`

What the client gives you:

| Call | What it does |
| :---- | :---- |
| `run(queue, job, timeout=..., grep=...)` | Submits a Job, waits for it to finish and returns its log (only the lines matching `grep`, if given). It raises an error when the Job fails, which fails the task. |
