| `serving(queue, workload, port)` | Starts a long-running server (a Deployment, StatefulSet or LeaderWorkerSet), waits until it is ready, gives you its URL, and deletes it when the `async with` block ends. Use it to serve a model once and send several checks at it. |
| `follow_logs(...)` | Yields a workload's log lines as they are written. |
| `submit`, `wait`, `workload_status`, `workload_logs`, `workload_delete` | The same tools an agent has, as methods, for anything the two helpers do not cover. |

`Client` has the same methods without `async`. Under the hood the task is handed a short-lived credential for each server it named (in the `CRUCIBLE_TASK_SERVERS` environment variable), and the client reads it for you. Cancelling a wait leaves the workload running, so set `activeDeadlineSeconds` on the Job as well.

The rules about names and manifests in the next part apply here too: the same queue, the same GPU `nodeSelector`, and a Job name that is unique to the run.

## Step 2 with an agent: the kueue tools

The agent calls the kueue tools in this order.

| Call | Why |
| :---- | :---- |
| `whoami` | Returns the run's identity, including `run_id`, and the namespace it may use. |
| `queues_list`, `hardware_describe` | What queues exist and what GPU models each offers. The agent picks the queue that has the model you asked for. |
| `workload_plan` with `queue` and `manifest` | A rehearsal. The server checks the Job, fills in what it adds, and says whether it fits: `fits_now`, `waits_for_quota` or `never_fits`. It returns a `plan_hash`. |
| `workload_submit` with the same `queue`, the same `manifest` and the `plan_hash` | Creates the Job. |
| `workload_status` with `kind`, `name` and `until: "finished"` | Waits for the Job. One call waits at most 50 seconds, so the agent repeats it until the Job has finished. |
| `workload_logs` with `kind` and `name` | What the Job printed. |

Rules that follow from how plan and submit work:

* Submit must send exactly what was planned. If the agent edits the manifest between the two calls, the hashes differ and the submit is refused.  
* Submitting the same plan twice is safe. The second call answers "already submitted".  
* A different manifest under a name that is already taken is a conflict. So give every Job a name that is unique to the run. A good recipe: a fixed word, a dash, and the first 8 characters of the SHA-256 of the `run_id` that `whoami` returned.  
* `never_fits` means the Job asks for more than the queue will ever have (too many GPUs, or a GPU model the queue does not offer). Stop there. Waiting does not help.

The manifest is the Job from What a GPU Job looks like on the Running on pirate tab, written as JSON. Put the whole thing in the prompt with a few placeholders, and tell the agent to change nothing else:

`{`  
  `"apiVersion": "batch/v1",`  
  `"kind": "Job",`  
  `"metadata": {"name": "NAME"},`  
  `"spec": {`  
    `"backoffLimit": 0,`  
    `"activeDeadlineSeconds": 3600,`  
    `"ttlSecondsAfterFinished": 7200,`  
    `"template": {"spec": {`  
      `"restartPolicy": "Never",`  
      `"nodeSelector": {"nvidia.com/gpu.product": "NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB"},`  
      `"containers": [{`  
        `"name": "main",`  
        `"image": "IMAGE",`  
        `"command": ["sh", "/opt/x/run.sh"],`  
        `"resources": {`  
          `"requests": {"cpu": "8", "memory": "64Gi", "nvidia.com/gpu": "1"},`  
          `"limits": {"cpu": "8", "memory": "64Gi", "nvidia.com/gpu": "1"}`  
        `}`  
      `}]`  
    `}}`  
  `}`  
`}`

What the fields that are new here do:

* `activeDeadlineSeconds` kills the Job after an hour, so a hung server cannot hold a GPU all night.  
* `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` deletes the finished Job two hours later, so old Jobs do not pile up.  
* `requests` and `limits` are the same. The Job gets exactly what it asks for.  
* `command` replaces the image's own start command. A vLLM image starts `vllm serve` by default, which never exits. A Job has to end.  
* There is no namespace and no queue label. The server adds both from the `queue` argument.

`workload_status` says how a wait ended:

| `ended` | Meaning | What the agent should do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `reached` | The Job got to the state asked for | Go on |
| `settled` | The Job finished or was stopped | Go on and read the log |
| `timeout` | 50 seconds passed | Call again |
| `stuck` | A pod has a serious problem (a bad image reference, for example) | Stop and record the status |

Tell the agent how long to keep waiting. A Job can queue for quota behind other teams, so 45 minutes is a reasonable limit, and the task's `timeout` must be longer than that.

The last thing the prompt asks for is a file holding the raw replies:

`{"job": "<NAME>", "queue": "<the queue>", "status": <the last workload_status reply>, "logs": <the workload_logs reply>}`

The task that wraps the prompt:

`bench = agent(`  
    `name = "bench",`  
    `prompt = prompt_file("prompts/kueue.md") + "\nGPU product: " + param("gpu_product") + "\n",`  
    `depends_on = [build],`  
    `isolated = True,`  
    `emits_files = ["kueue/job.json"],`  
    `timeout = "70m",`  
`)`

`depends_on = [build]` puts `inputs/build/results/build.json` in the agent's workspace, which is where it reads the image reference. `isolated = True` gives the turn its own copy of the workspace, so two such tasks can run at the same time without writing over each other's `kueue/job.json`.

## Step 3: check the result in a script

Have the program inside the Job print one line that starts with a fixed word followed by JSON, for example:

`result {"completed": 200, "output_throughput": 1843.2, "mean_ttft_ms": 41.7}`

An `evaluate` task then finds that line in `inputs/bench/kueue/job.json`, parses it and decides. If the line is missing, it prints the Job's status, which is where the reason is. An `evaluate` task that exits non-zero fails the run, so the pass mark is enforced by the script and not by the agent's opinion.

## Worked example: vllm-build-bench-eval

Lucas Wilkinson's draft `vllm-build-bench-eval` is this shape end to end, with agent turns for the run step, and it is the best pack to copy for build-then-measure work. It builds vLLM at any GitHub ref, runs a benchmark and a GSM8K accuracy check at the same time as two Jobs, and returns the benchmark only when accuracy holds.

`build    command   buildit runs image/build.sh over a vLLM release image and pushes one new layer`  
  `|- bench   agent   runs the image as a Kueue Job, copies its status and log`  
  `|- gsm8k   agent   the same, with the accuracy check`  
       `verify  evaluate  GSM8K accuracy >= min_gsm8k and all 200 benchmark requests finished`

What is in the pack:

| File | What it is |
| :---- | :---- |
| `crucible.toml` | Injects `image/` into the workspace and sets the sandbox image. |
| `workflow.star` | The four tasks and six params (`vllm_repo`, `vllm_ref`, `base_image`, `gpu_product`, `model`, `min_gsm8k`). |
| `vllm_build.star` | A reusable `vllm_build()` function that returns the build task. Copy it with `image/build.sh` and you have the build in one line. |
| `image/build.sh` | Runs inside the base image. Checks out the ref, applies any `image/patches/*.patch`, and installs vLLM into `/opt/crucible/venv`. It reuses published compiled kernels when the ref's C++ and CUDA sources match a published wheel, and compiles them (through ccache) when they do not. |
| `image/run.sh` | Runs inside the Job. Starts `vllm serve`, waits until it is healthy, runs the check, prints one `result {...}` line and exits. |
| `prompts/kueue.md` | The fixed recipe from Step 2\. One prompt serves both Jobs. The mode (`bench` or `gsm8k`) is appended to it. |

Things it does that are worth copying:

* One prompt, two tasks. A small Starlark function (`on_kueue(mode)`) makes an agent task per mode, so adding a third check is one line.  
* The two Jobs run at the same time, each in an isolated turn.  
* To change vLLM's code, either point `vllm_repo` and `vllm_ref` at a fork, or drop a `git diff` into `image/patches/`.  
* `verify` prints a one-line summary (commit, accuracy, time to ready, throughput, time to first token) as the run's result.

To try it, copy it to a draft of your own and launch that:

`crux draft-clone vllm-build-bench-eval jdoe-build-bench-eval`

`crux draft-launch jdoe-build-bench-eval --dispatch-target pirate --provider enmaas --model rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --max-cost 10 --max-time 3h --params '{"vllm_ref":"main"}'`

Read the pack before you run it (`crux draft-pull vllm-build-bench-eval ./bbe`). The build task allows 75 minutes and each Job task 70\.

The other reference is `examples/optimize-loop` in the core repo, where the agent does the building too and iterates. The hill climb on the next tab is the GPU version of that.

## When it goes wrong

| What you see | Likely cause | What to do |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `buildit: command not found`, or the agent has no buildit or kueue tools | The run is not on pirate | Launch with `--dispatch-target pirate` |
| A command task's `crucible_kueue` call fails with no server configured | `servers = ["kueue"]` is missing from `[workflow]` | Add it |
| The build hangs on a download | The step uses plain `http://` | Use `https://` |
| `buildit build` refuses the context | The task is isolated, or the directory is not in `[workspace] inject` | Build from a task that is not isolated, and inject the directory |
| `workload_plan` says `never_fits` | More GPUs than the queue has, or a GPU model it does not offer | Fix the request |
| `workload_submit` is refused with two hashes | The manifest changed after the plan | Tell the agent to send the planned manifest unchanged |
| `workload_submit` reports a conflict | The Job name is already used by a different manifest | Make the name unique to the run |
| The Job stays pending | Waiting for GPU quota | Wait, or check the queue (`oc get workloads -n crucible-kueue-e2e`) |
| Status says `stuck` with an image pull error | The image was never pushed, or the reference is wrong | Check that the build task ran `buildit push` and that the Job uses its `image` |
| The verify task says the Job printed no result line | The program in the Job failed before printing | Read the status and log in `kueue/job.json` under the Files pane |
| The Job is killed at its deadline | `activeDeadlineSeconds` is shorter than the work | Raise it, and the task `timeout` with it |

# Hill climb example

`examples/vllm-hill-climb` in the core repo (PR [https\://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible/pull/355](https://github.com/neuralmagic/crucible/pull/355), not merged yet; branch `claude/vllm-hill-climb-pack`) is the reference for a GPU workflow on pirate. [vLLM](https://docs.vllm.ai/) is an inference server for large language models. In it, an agent makes vLLM's fused MoE path faster on an A100. It proposes an edit, builds it, measures it on a GPU, keeps it only if it is faster and still correct, and repeats.

`seed    (command) build vLLM at vllm_ref once through buildit, push it; count ccache hits`  
  `-> climb (agent)  baseline, then N rounds of 2-3 candidates; each built as a layer over the seed`  
                    `and measured as a Kueue Job on an A100; keeps the fastest correct one`  
     `-> report (command) speedup, per-step times, build reuse -> summary.md`

What to copy from it:

* Deterministic ends. The expensive one-off build (`seed`) and the report are commands. Only the climb, which needs judgment, is an agent.  
* A frozen measurement. `build/bench/moe_bench.py` is injected (frozen), checks every output against a float32 reference, and prints one machine-readable line (`hill-climb-result {...}`). The agent cannot edit what measures it.  
* Cheap candidates. `hc.py stage` builds Python-only edits as a single layer over the seed image, with nothing compiled. C++ and CUDA edits rebuild with the shared ccache.  
* Explicit GPU placement. Every Job carries a `nodeSelector` for `nvidia.com/gpu.product: NVIDIA-A100-SXM4-80GB`, so every measurement runs on the same GPU model.  
* Files as the record. The climb emits `report.json`, `timeline.jsonl`, `results.jsonl` and `best.patch`, and the report reads them from `inputs/climb/`.

Run it yourself:

1\. Check out the branch and drop `examples/vllm-hill-climb` on the desktop app (it creates the draft and opens its launch form), or push it with `crux` under your own draft id.

2\. Launch on `pirate`, provider `enmaas`, model `rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017`, max time 3h, max cost about \$40.

`crux draft-launch jdoe-vllm-hill-climb --dispatch-target pirate --provider enmaas --model rits/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 --max-cost 40 --max-time 3h`

3\. Expect the seed to take several minutes, because it compiles vLLM (the shared ccache helps a lot). Expect the first A100 Job to spend a while pulling the \~20 GB image.

4\. Read `report/summary.md` in the Files pane, or `crux run-file <run_id> report/summary.md`. `climb/best.patch` is the kept diff.

Recent result: run 4 kept a 1.06x fused MoE speedup, with the serving check at \+0.6% output throughput.

The pack's own tests:

`cargo test -p crucible --test vllm_hill_climb_example`

# Debugging runs

## Where to look

| Question | Desktop app | Web UI | crux |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Is it running? What did it cost? | Sidebar, run header | `/playbook-runs` | `crux playbook-runs` |
| Which task failed? | Tasks pane, Graph pane | Launch page graph | `crux graph <run_id>` |
| What did it print? | Log pane (by task) | Task drill-down | `crux run-log <run_id> -f` |
| What did the agent do? | Transcript pane | Run page live session | `crux run-session <run_id>` |
| What files did it produce? | Files pane | Run page Files | `crux run-files`, `crux run-file` |
| Compare fan-out instances | Compare pane |  |  |

![][image14]

*The Graph pane: the task graph, colored by result.*

![][image15]

*The Timeline pane: when each task started and how long it took.*

![][image16]

*The Launch pane: what this run was launched with (provider, model, ceilings, draft version) and the cluster and pod it ran in.*

## Reading a failure

1\. Look at the graph first and find the first red task. A task that never ran is one whose dependency did not pass.

2\. Search the log for that task's `[<task>]` prefix.

3\. Check the usual causes, in this order: a missing declared field (the agent never wrote `PLAN_TASK_RESULT.json`, or a command printed something after its JSON line), a missing declared file, a script that was not injected (`can't open file`), a task timeout longer than the launch's `--max-time`, or a provider or model that does not match the image's harness.

Timing notes:

* `run-log -f` is the only live view. `graph` and `run-files` are written when the run is ingested, so mid-run they return 404 or come back empty.  
* A command is silent in the log until it finishes. Minutes of nothing during a build is normal.  
* The pod's `verdict:` line arrives up to a minute before the controller has ingested the run. Wait for `-- run <id> is <status>`.  
* If `run-log -f` exits with `connection closed before message completed`, the run is fine. Run the command again to reattach.

![][image17]

*Reading a failure. The red banner is the run's error. The failed task's card expands to show its inputs, with buttons to jump to its log lines or transcript.*

## Rerun from a task

Fix the pack, push it, then rerun only from the failed task. Results from earlier tasks are reused if their compiled definitions did not change.

`crux draft-launch jdoe-mypack --rerun-of <run_id> --from <task> --dispatch-target pirate --provider enmaas --model rits/zai-org/glm-5-3 --max-cost 5 --max-time 1h`

In the app, use **Rerun from here** on the task card. It shows which tasks will be reused and offers "Rerun those too" for tasks that changed.

![][image18]

*Rerun from here. The dialog lists what will be reused and what will run again, and lets you change the target, model and ceilings first.*

## Cancel

* App: Cancel in the run header (press twice).  
* CLI: `crux cancel <key>`.  
* Web UI: Cancel on the launch page.

Cancel parks the launch and deletes its running pods. It is how you stop spend.

# Going further

* Graduate a draft to a playbook: use Graduate in Draft Studio, or `crux draft-graduate`. Publishing lands the pack in a Git repo and registers it, so your team can launch it.  
* Schedules: launch on a cron schedule from the launch form ("On a schedule") in the app or the web UI. A schedule stores its target, provider and model. Use a schedule cursor to carry state between firings (see the draft-a-playbook skill in `crucible-domains/skills/`).  
* Webhooks and watches: start a launch from an external event or a tracker query.  
* Local controller: `just controller-local` in a core checkout runs a controller on your laptop with embedded Postgres, so you can develop packs with no cluster.  
* More examples (`examples/` in core): `playbook` (no-cost litmus), `triage` (skill, fan-out, report), `revise-loop`, `route`, `human-gate`, `schema-repair`, `action-pins` (secrets and PRs), `git-smoke` (pushing as a GitHub App), `optimize-loop` (buildit plus Kueue, the smaller sibling of the hill climb), `vllm-agent-build`, `vllm-build-bench`.  
* Domain packs in `crucible-domains/domains/`: real production packs (CVE triage, backports, vLLM).

# Desktop app

## Layout

* Sidebar: one row per playbook, showing its newest launch, with running launches first. Filters: search, owner (All / Just mine), origin (All / Schedules / Drafts), landed (1h / 24h / 7d). A playbook with many launches opens a runs page (pass rate, spend, timeline, 12-week heatmap).  
* Run view: dockable panes for Tasks, Timeline, Graph, Data, Files, Transcript, Compare, Pack, Launch and Log. ⌘1 to ⌘8 jump to them. Revise rounds show as "round N of M", separate from fan-out instances.  
* Files pane: captured files by task, with Markdown rendered, patches shown as diffs and JSON indented. Files over 8 MiB show the `crux run-file` command instead.  
* Pack pane: the pack's files with `crucible-lsp` diagnostics. Files open in your external editor (VS Code, Cursor, Zed or a custom command).  
* Run finder (⌘⇧F): full-text search across every run of a pack.  
* Management pages: Schedules, Secrets, Decisions (⌘⇧D, answer human routes), Approvals, Shares, Settings.

## Things only the app does

* Multiple controllers as profiles, switched with ⌘⌥1..9, including SSH or SOCKS tunnels per profile.  
* Drag a pack folder onto the Dock icon to push and test-fire it.  
* Notifications when your launches finish or a decision is waiting, a Dock badge for pending decisions and approvals, and a menu bar list of running launches across profiles.  
* Fix with agent briefs (see the Authoring loop tab).  
* Offline cache: the app shows the last copy of everything when the controller is unreachable.

## Limits today

Checked against v0.6.4. Most of what the app lacked at v0.6.0 has shipped: the launch form picks the target, provider and model, the Files pane is in, there is a Fedora build, color codes are stripped from log lines, and the app has the controller's management pages (API keys, Teams, Triggers with schedules and webhooks, Providers, Blueprints, Activity, Issues, and Admin with a Policy tab).

What is left:

* Pack files are edited in your own editor, not in the app. The app opens the file, checks it and saves the draft.  
* No publishing or graduating a draft, and no starting an import. Use the web UI or `crux` for those. (Approving or discarding a pending import is in the app.)  
* The sidebar lists a playbook by its newest launch, so one that has never launched is not there. Open it with ⌘K or a link. A draft that has never run opens its launch form.  
* Only playbooks are listed. Scored loops (autoresearch runs) are not.  
* A run on a spoke cluster (pirate, pirate 2\) streams through its pod's log. A very long log line can arrive only when the run ends.  
* On Fedora the Dock badge, the menu bar item and folder drops do nothing.  
* The management pages are new in v0.6.2. Their buttons that change things (minting, adding a member, editing a provider) have had less use than the rest of the app. If one misbehaves, the web UI has the same action.

# Costs and limits

* Every launch sets a cost ceiling and a time ceiling. Today's caps per launch: \$50 and 3h (`crux playbook-caps`). There is also a shared daily budget for the whole deployment.  
* Ask for what the run needs, not the cap. The ceiling is what stops a runaway, and spend is booked to you.  
* Command tasks still run after the cost ceiling is hit. The time ceiling stops everything.  
* Use a cheap model while iterating (`rits/zai-org/glm-5-3`) and move to a stronger one once the pack works.  
* Do not hold GPUs. Make GPU Jobs exit when done, and delete stray ones (`workload_delete`, or `oc` if you are a submitter).  
* Name drafts `<you>-<thing>` and delete the ones you are finished with.

# Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Cause | Fix |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| `/playbooks` is empty | Not in `tibrahim-all` | Get added, then sign out and back in |
| `crux whoami` says `credential: bearer (anonymous)` | Token is not a `crk_` key (truncated paste) | Re-paste the key |
| `401 ... not one this controller issued` | Wrong controller or truncated key | Check `url` is the `crucible-api...` host |
| `401 ... expired` or `revoked` | Old key | Mint a new one on `/settings` |
| 403 right after being granted access | Groups come from your last browser sign-in | Sign in to the web UI again and mint a new key |
| Launch refused: timeout longer than `--max-time` | A task's `timeout` exceeds the launch ceiling | Raise `--max-time` or lower the task timeout |
| Launch refused naming the cap | Asked for more than \$50 or 3h | Ask for less |
| Launch refused naming a secret | Secret declared but not bound to this draft | `crux secret-bind ... --playbook <draft>` |
| First agent turn fails at 0 tokens | No model pin on `enmaas`, or harness/image mismatch | Pin `--provider enmaas --model rits/...` and match the image to the harness |
| Task fails `output missing declared field` | Agent did not write `PLAN_TASK_RESULT.json`, or a command printed after its JSON | Name the file and keys in the prompt, and send progress to stderr |
| `can't open file` in a command | Script not in `[workspace] inject` | Inject it |
| Fan-out task fails on a long list | `max_fanout` is an assertion | Bound the producer and set `max_fanout` to that bound |
| Agent says a tool is not permitted | Binary not in `[agent.openshell] binaries` | Add the absolute path |
| `draft-push` refused | Someone saved a newer version | `crux draft-pull` into a fresh directory and reconcile |
| GPU Job pending forever | The queue is full, or the `nodeSelector` matches no node with a free GPU | Run `oc get workloads -n crucible-kueue-e2e` and `oc describe pod <pod>`, and read the Events |
| GPU Job ran on a B200 | The Job has no `nodeSelector` on `nvidia.com/gpu.product` | Add it (see the Job example on the Running on pirate tab) |
| `graph` or `run-files` 404 mid-run | Written only at ingest | Use `run-log -f` until the run settles |
| Draft not in the desktop sidebar | Never launched | ⌘K, or `crucible-playbooks://playbook/<id>` |
| App will not open on macOS | Quarantine flag | `xattr -d com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Crucible Playbooks.app"` |
